newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Foreign investors seen lukewarm about Seoul bourse.
newsitem.headline: Foreign investors seen lukewarm about Seoul bourse.

text.p: Foreign fund managers, worried about getting bogged down in a lacklustre Seoul stock market, are likely to be picky when South Korea raises the ceiling for overseas investors on Tuesday, analysts said on Monday.

"I think there will be some very selective buying in stocks that are either in structurally attractive sectors like telecommunications, or are deemed to be insulated from a general deteriorating macroeconomic and operating environment," said Stephen Marvin, head of research at SsangYong Investment and Securities Co.
"But I think there is going to be much less interest in traditional blue chips than has been the case in the past," he said.
From Tuesday, foreign investors will be able to purchase up to 20 percent of most stocks, up from the current 18 percent.

Companies considered strategically important to the national economy, such as steel manufacturer Pohang Iron and Steel Co Ltd (POSCO) and Korea Electric Power Corp (KEPCO), will be boosted to 15 percent from 12 percent.
South Korean shares ended lower on Monday as domestic investors began to worry that foreigners would not rescusitate the doldrum-stricken market. The composite stock index fell 3.54 points to 789.67.
Analysts had predicted that foreigners would inject between one and two trillion won ($1.21 billion-$2.42 billion) into the bourse, but some market watchers felt this was too optimistic.
"I'm worried that the immediate inflow may not even reach 500 billion won," said a local fund manager.
Brokers added that signs of interest from foreign fund managers ahead of the ceiling boost was less than had been seen during previous ceiling increases.

"Many are waiting till after the market closes in order not to tip off local investors, but still, the number of phone calls inquiring about stock this time is much less," said Jay Kwon of First Securities.
Some analysts suggested that the best bargains would come to those who wait.
"Don't come charging in," advised John Pinkel, director of HG Asia Securities in Seoul. "Wait, because quite a few shares will become cheaper."

Depositary receipts held overseas means the nation's largest mobile telecommunications company, Korea Mobile Telecom, and Kookmin Bank have already hit their maximum foreign shareholder ceilings, while direct foreign investment in blue chip Shinhan Bank has blacked out further overseas shareholdings.
POSCO is also up to its foreign limit.
What were some of the picks for Tuesday?
"I think Sungmi Telecom will be one of the hottest shares," said Richard Kim, a broker at KLB Securities. "It is the leader in CDMA (code division multiple access) technology."
Samsung Fire and Marine, a unit of the Samsung Group, was also expected to attract a lot of interest as a top-tier insurance firm a with huge reserve.
"To any investor seeking absolute profits, I would suggest he put nothing in Korea," said Marvin.

For institutional investors interested in beating the KOSPI index, Marvin suggested Housing and Commercial Bank, which has a low exposure to guaranteed yield trust accounts and stock market investments.
